tweets.text:
I’ve been working with Claude Code since it was released and have developed a workflow that lets me safely manage multiple streams of work in parallel. This is a deep dive into how it works. At a high level, I:

- Parallelize my work streams through extensive use of git worktrees
- Mitigate LLM "doom loops" through a a two-step development process that keeps work grounded in a clear specification
- Automate the entire process through the use of Claude Code’s custom slash commands.

Deep Dive

First off, this is how I structure my workspace:

When I start Claude Code, I start it within the `repo-env` directory so it can manage worktrees. The custom Claude commands orchestrate this.

Aside: In case you're unfamiliar with the concept, a git "worktree" is basically a branch backed by a folder containing an entire copy of the repository. You can have any number of these, effectively letting you work in multiple branches at once without having to commit/stash the changes before switching.

Begin by writing a task

I’ll begin a session by writing a task. This is one of the few things I’ll write manually if it’s sufficiently complex. Otherwise, I’ll ask Claude Code to write the task for me after providing context, like background and rationale for the feature/fix, relevant files to investigate, web URLs, etc. I’ll iterate on this until I’m happy with the result.

Start a task
 
After the task is in good shape I use /project:start-task with the name of the markdown file as an argument to the task (which is not necessary if I haven’t cleared out the context; Claude will figure it out in that case). This command:

- Ensures that the main branch on the git repo is up to date
- Creates the worktree if it doesn’t already exist
- Performs any repository-specific setup (e.g. npm install)
- Loads context:
  - Reads the task file
  - Reads the last five commits
- Instructs Claude to record design decisions in the task document
- Begins implementation

If the task is complex, I’ll review each edit. If it’s fairly straightforward I’ll turn on auto-accept. If the task spans multiple sessions, I’ll use /project:orient with the task name as an argument, which performs the above context-loading steps to get itself up to speed.

Complete the task

After the implementation is finished and I’ve verified the results either manually, via automated testing, or a combination of both, I’ll run /project:complete-task. This command:

- Checks for uncommitted changes in the worktree, asking me for input on committing them if so.
- Updates the task to indicate completion
- Depending on the project, either:
  - Push the branch to main and open a PR, or
  - Merge the branch into main and clean up the worktree

This workflow has some major advantages:

- Using worktrees keeps the vibes contained.
- I can manage multiple streams of work in parallel, usually up to about three.
- Custom slash commands:
  - Can be customized on a per-project basis
  - Make dealing with worktrees really easy

The hardest part of this process is in writing good task specifications, but worktrees make gracefully handling poor tasks straightforward: delete the worktree, improve the task, and try again.

That’s the gist of it. Feel free to reach out if you’ve got questions or need some help getting set up!
